sweep_summary: Polish (poli1260) is in the catalog as fixed-strict penultimate, deciding quote 'Stress is generally penultimate (Hyman 1977:39)' via StressTyp2; the record already carries a check against Rubach & Booij 1985 (Lingua 66, 'primary stress in Polish falls on the penult') and Oliver & Grice 2003. Of the 23 title hits, 7 are about Polish word stress (Kraska-Szlenk 1995/2003, Newlin-Łukowicz 2012, Awedyk 1986, Comrie 1976, Madelska & Dressler 1996, Franks 1985; Demenko 1999 and the two Bański works unclear), 7 are prosody-but-not-word-stress (sentence stress, intonation, boundaries, glottalisation, sandhi), 4 are L2-English studies, and Gretser 1593 is a Greek grammar mis-linked to Polish. Nothing read contradicts penultimate placement: the Newlin-Łukowicz abstract (paywalled, abstract captured) says simple words have a single penultimate prominence and argues against phonetic secondary stress; Wojtkowiak & Schwartz 2018 (downloaded, open) use 'the stressed penultimate vowel' as baseline; Jassem 2003 (JIPA illustration, held by the project, read) gives the fullest first-hand statement: penultimate with listed antepenultimate exceptions (Classical loans, some proper names, scattered native words, regularized under inflection) and initial secondary stress — this refines the 'strict' qualifier and is a better deciding citation than Hyman 1977:39. Łukaszewicz 2018 (Phonology 35, held by the project) restates 'main stress on the penult' and Dłuska 1932's initial/penultimate anchoring. Web search by automated download was exhausted/blocked ( 2000/2000; DDG/Mojeek/S2/archive. De Gruyter bot-check), so Kraska-Szlenk, Comrie 1976 (International Review of Slavic Linguistics 1:227-240, print), Franks 1985 (JSTOR), Awedyk 1986 and Madelska & Dressler 1996 (De Gruyter, paywalled) remain unread; Kraska-Szlenk and Comrie are the high-priority acquisitions for the exception classes.

new_statements.quote: Lexical stress (potential for phrasal accent) usually falls on the penultimate syllable, but there are various exceptions with antepenultimate stress, such as some lexemes derived from the Classical languages or some fully 'Polonized' foreign proper names: fonetyka 'phonetics' or 'phonetician (gen. sing.)', prezydent 'president', Waszyngton, Jerozolima. Allolexes of such lexemes with an added syllable in the ending are, however, 'regular'; e.g. fonetykami 'phoneticians (instr. pl)'. There are also scattered native exceptions: rzeczpospolita 'republic', okolica 'neighbourhood', etc. Secondary lexical stress falls on the initial syllable in lexemes of four or more syllables

sources.quote: Word-initial syllables in standard Polish typically bear some degree of phonetic prominence (Dogil 1999). This prominence is not, we claim, due to secondary stress, but rather serves as a boundary marker (Newlin-Łukowicz 2012) that maintains the prosodic integrity of words. [...] the relative prominence of the initial vowel to the stressed penultimate vowel.
sources.note: Takes penultimate main stress as given ('the stressed penultimate vowel', used as the baseline in the prominence measures) and treats initial-syllable prominence as a boundary effect rather than secondary stress.
